title: Tool Description Engineering & Actionable Errors
scopeHtml: Scope: Writing tool instructions models use correctly, and errors that help an agent recover.

notes.title: Why a tool description is a prompt
notes.html:
A tool (also called a function) is a capability you hand to a language model: "search orders", "refund a payment", "read a file". The model cannot see your code. All it ever sees is a small text package for each tool: a name, a description, and a schema (a JSON Schema listing the parameters, their types and which are required). From those three things alone the model must decide (1) whether to call the tool at all, (2) which tool out of many, and (3) what values to put in each parameter.

So a tool description is not documentation for a human. It is a prompt, read by a reader that has no context, cannot ask you questions, and will take every word literally. A vague description gives you vague behaviour: the wrong tool gets called, parameters are guessed, or the tool is never called.

 Your code                      What the model sees
 -----------------              ---------------------------------
 def search_orders(...)   -->   name:        search_orders
   (hundreds of lines)          description: "Finds orders..."
                                input_schema: {customer_id: string, ...}
                                (nothing else. No code, no README.)

The same is true of the tool result that comes back. The model reads it as text and uses it to choose the next step. An error message is therefore also a prompt: it is the only instruction the model gets about what to do after a failure. This note has two halves: writing descriptions that make the model call tools correctly, and writing errors that let the model recover. See also (C5 01_A1) "Designing tools" and "Tool errors and recovery" for the short checklists; here we go deeper on wording, schemas, numbers, code and failure modes.

A rough mental model of the cost: Anthropic documents that tool definitions are added to the prompt (a hidden system section), so they cost input tokens on every request (verify exact overhead in the docs). A 300-token description on 20 tools is 6,000 tokens per call before the user has said anything. Good descriptions are complete but not bloated.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: imagine hiring a temp worker on day one and leaving them only labelled buttons on a machine. If the labels say "Go" and "Do", they will press the wrong one. If the machine beeps with no message, they are stuck. Descriptions are the labels; errors are the beeps that should say what to do next.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the model reads my function" is wrong: it reads only name, description and schema.
  • Treating the description as optional. Many providers allow omitting it, but quality drops sharply; it is the main routing signal.
  • Forgetting that every tool definition costs tokens on every request, so "more detail everywhere" is not free.

notes.title: Anatomy of a good tool description
notes.html:
A useful description answers six questions in plain sentences. Write them as short paragraphs or sentences, not as a keyword list.

  1. What does it do? One sentence, concrete verb and object.
  2. When should it be used? The situations that should trigger it, in the user's words.
  3. When should it NOT be used? Name the neighbouring tool that handles those cases.
  4. What does each parameter mean? Format, units, allowed values, an example.
  5. What does it return? Shape, size limits, what "empty" means, which ids can be used in follow-up calls.
  6. What are the side effects and limits? Read-only or writes; cost; rate limits; permissions.

Compare a weak and a strong description of the same tool.

WEAK
  name: search
  description: "Searches the database."

STRONG
  name: search_orders
  description:
    "Look up a customer's past orders by customer id and optional date range.
     Use this when the user asks about order history, delivery status or
     'what did I buy'. Do NOT use it to look up products (use search_products)
     or to change an order (use cancel_order). Returns at most 20 orders,
     newest first, each with order_id, status, total_cents and created_at.
     If there are more, the result says has_more=true and gives next_cursor.
     Read-only: it never changes data."

What each sentence buys you: the "use when" phrase maps user language to the tool; "do NOT use" removes confusion with search_products; "at most 20" tells the model it may need to paginate; "read-only" tells it that calling it speculatively is safe.

Length guidance: Anthropic's tool-use guidance stresses that detailed descriptions are the single most important factor in tool performance, and recommends several sentences (3-4 or more for non-trivial tools) over a one-liner (verify the exact wording in the current docs). Do not pad: each sentence should change a decision the model makes.

A good test: give the description to a colleague who has never seen your codebase and ask them to call the tool by hand. Where they hesitate, the model will too.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a good label on a medicine bottle says what it treats, the dose, when not to take it, and side effects. "Pills" tells you nothing.

Common interview traps.

  • "Short descriptions save tokens so they are better": false economy. A wrong tool call costs a whole extra round trip, far more than 80 extra tokens.
  • Describing how the code is implemented (database, framework) instead of what the model needs to decide.
  • Forgetting the negative guidance ("do not use for...") when two tools overlap.

notes.title: Names, parameters and schemas the model can use
notes.html:
The name is read by the model too. Use verb_noun in snake_case or camelCase, consistently: get_order_status, cancel_order, list_invoices. Avoid generic names (run, query, data). Many APIs restrict the characters (for Anthropic, names are limited to letters, digits, underscores and hyphens and a maximum length; verify the exact regex in the docs). When tools come from several systems, prefix with a namespace: crm_search_contacts, billing_search_invoices. Prefixes help both humans reading logs and the model choosing among near-duplicates.

Parameters are where most wrong calls originate. Rules that work:

  • Describe every parameter, not just the tool. A description field per property is free routing information.
  • Use enums for closed sets: "status": {"enum": ["open", "shipped", "cancelled"]}. The model will then not invent "in_transit".
  • State formats with an example: "date": "ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2025-03-14".
  • State units: amount_cents (integer) beats amount (is it dollars, a float, a string?).
  • Mark required vs optional honestly, and give defaults in the text ("default 20, max 100").
  • Prefer flat parameters to deeply nested objects; nested optional structures are where models drop fields.
  • Avoid parameters the model cannot know. If a tool needs internal_user_uuid, either supply it in code (from the session) or give the model a lookup tool. Never make the model guess an id.
  • Do not expose parameters the model should not control, such as user_id for the current user. Inject them server side. That is also a security rule: the model must not be able to ask for another user's data.
  • Fewer parameters is better. Each additional parameter is another chance for a mistake. Merge or default where you can.

A tool definition in the Anthropic Messages API is a JSON object with name, description and input_schema (a JSON Schema). Here it is in all three languages. The Python block uses the real SDK shape; the Kotlin and Java blocks build the same schema as plain data, so the tool side is visible without depending on a particular SDK helper (the Java SDK has its own builder types; verify them in the SDK docs).

# What it shows: a tool definition dict passed as tools=[...] to client.messages.create
search_orders_tool = {
    "name": "search_orders",
    "description": (
        "Look up a customer's past orders. Use for order history or delivery "
        "status questions. Do NOT use for product lookup (search_products). "
        "Returns up to 20 orders, newest first, with order_id, status, "
        "total_cents, created_at. Read-only."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "customer_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer id like 'cus_8412'. Use lookup_customer if you only have an email."},
            "status": {"type": "string", "enum": ["open", "shipped", "cancelled"], "description": "Optional filter."},
            "since": {"type": "string", "description": "Optional ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2025-03-14."},
        },
        "required": ["customer_id"],
    },
}
// What it shows: the same definition as plain Kotlin maps; serialise to JSON for the REST call
// (or map into the Java SDK's tool builder; verify type names in the SDK docs).
val searchOrdersTool = mapOf(
    "name" to "search_orders",
    "description" to "Look up a customer's past orders. Use for order history or delivery " +
        "status questions. Do NOT use for product lookup (search_products). " +
        "Returns up to 20 orders, newest first. Read-only.",
    "input_schema" to mapOf(
        "type" to "object",
        "properties" to mapOf(
            "customer_id" to mapOf("type" to "string", "description" to "Customer id like 'cus_8412'."),
            "status" to mapOf("type" to "string", "enum" to listOf("open", "shipped", "cancelled")),
            "since" to mapOf("type" to "string", "description" to "Optional ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2025-03-14."),
        ),
        "required" to listOf("customer_id"),
    ),
)
// What it shows: the same definition with Map.of; serialise with Jackson/Gson for the REST call
// (or use anthropic-java's tool types; verify names in the SDK docs).
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

Map<String, Object> searchOrdersTool = Map.of(
    "name", "search_orders",
    "description", "Look up a customer's past orders. Use for order history or delivery "
        + "status questions. Do NOT use for product lookup (search_products). "
        + "Returns up to 20 orders, newest first. Read-only.",
    "input_schema", Map.of(
        "type", "object",
        "properties", Map.of(
            "customer_id", Map.of("type", "string", "description", "Customer id like 'cus_8412'."),
            "status", Map.of("type", "string", "enum", List.of("open", "shipped", "cancelled")),
            "since", Map.of("type", "string", "description", "Optional ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2025-03-14.")),
        "required", List.of("customer_id")));

Real systems: OpenAI function calling, Anthropic tool use, Gemini function declarations and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) all use the same idea (name, description, JSON Schema). Some providers offer a strict mode that forces output to match the schema (verify availability per provider); it fixes malformed JSON but not wrong values, so descriptions still matter.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a paper form with tick boxes and examples ("DD/MM/YYYY") gets cleaner answers than a blank page that says "Enter details".

Common interview traps.

  • "A JSON Schema guarantees correct arguments": it constrains shape, not meaning. customer_id: "abc" is valid yet wrong.
  • Letting the model supply identity fields like user_id; that is an authorization hole, not a convenience.
  • Using free-text strings where an enum would remove a whole class of errors.

notes.title: Teaching the model when to pick which tool
notes.html:
When you have many tools, the hard problem is not calling a tool, it is choosing one. Models choose by comparing descriptions against the user request. Overlapping descriptions produce coin flips.

Techniques:

  1. Draw boundaries in the text. For each pair of confusable tools, each description names the other. "Use get_order_status for ONE known order id. Use search_orders to find orders when you do not have an id."
  2. Order of operations hints. "Call lookup_customer first to get a customer_id." This turns hidden prerequisites into visible ones.
  3. Merge near-duplicates. Three tools search_by_name, search_by_email, search_by_phone are usually one search_customer with a field enum.
  4. Split tools with different risk. A single manage_order(action=...) that can read and cancel hides risk. Separate get_order (read) from cancel_order (destructive) so permissions and approvals attach to the tool.
  5. Put overall policy in the system prompt, details in the tool. The system prompt says "always confirm before cancelling"; the tool description says what cancel_order needs.
  6. Add input examples where a parameter is non-obvious. One or two concrete examples in the parameter description often beat a paragraph of rules. (Anthropic documents an optional input-examples feature on tool definitions at the time of writing; verify in the docs before relying on it.)

How many tools? There is no magic number, but accuracy of selection tends to drop as the list grows and the definitions eat context. Common practice is to keep the visible set small (roughly under 20 per agent is a rule of thumb many teams use; treat as a heuristic, not a limit) and to use tool search / deferred tool loading for large sets: the model first sees only names and one-liners, then loads full schemas for the few it needs. Claude Code itself defers rarely used tools this way. Another option is routing: a cheap first step picks a subset of tools relevant to the request, then the agent runs with just those.

 50 tools x 250 tokens = 12,500 tokens in every request   (50 * 250 = 12,500)
 With routing/tool search showing 8 tools:
 8 x 250 = 2,000 tokens                                     (8 * 250 = 2,000)
 Saved per request: 10,500 input tokens, plus fewer wrong picks.

Failure pattern: "the model never calls my new tool". Usual causes: the description does not mention the user's phrasing; an older, broader tool already covers it; the system prompt tells the model to answer from its own knowledge. Fix the text first, not the model.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: in a hospital, signage says "Radiology: X-rays and scans. For blood tests go to Pathology." Each sign names the neighbour.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing more tools equals more capability. Past a point selection accuracy falls and cost rises.
  • Writing descriptions in isolation; confusion only shows when you read them side by side.
  • Hiding read and write behaviours behind one tool with an action flag.

notes.title: Testing and iterating on descriptions
notes.html:
Descriptions are code, so test them. Nobody gets them right first time, and they regress when a new tool is added.

Method:

  1. Build a small eval set: 20-50 realistic user requests, each with the expected tool and expected key arguments (or "no tool"). Include confusing cases: two plausible tools, missing required info, a request that should be refused.
  2. Run each request against the model with all tool definitions, but do not execute the tools. Just record which tool and arguments the model chose.
  3. Score: correct tool, correct arguments, correct "ask a question instead" decisions.
  4. Read the failures. Fix the description (not the test). Re-run everything, because a change that fixes one tool can break another.
  5. Keep the eval in CI so that adding a tool re-checks all routing.

Anthropic describes using Claude itself to help improve tool descriptions: feed it the tool definition plus transcripts of failures and ask for a revision (verify the current guidance). Treat the output as a draft and re-run the eval.

Here is a minimal routing eval. It calls the model and checks only the first tool the model asks for.

# What it prints: pass/fail per case, then the accuracy. Needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the env.
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
TOOLS = [search_orders_tool]    # add every tool you ship, plus a lookup tool etc.

CASES = [
    ("Where is my last order? I'm cus_8412", "search_orders"),
    ("Do you sell red sneakers?", None),  # no matching tool: expect plain text
]

passed = 0
for prompt, expected in CASES:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",  # verify model id in the docs
        max_tokens=512,
        tools=TOOLS,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    calls = [b.name for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    got = calls[0] if calls else None
    ok = got == expected
    passed += ok
    print("PASS" if ok else "FAIL", prompt, "->", got)
print(f"accuracy {passed}/{len(CASES)}")
// What it shows: the eval skeleton. The model call is behind callModel() which you implement
// with the Java SDK or an OkHttp POST to /v1/messages; it returns the first tool name or null.
data class Case(val prompt: String, val expectedTool: String?)

fun runEval(cases: List<Case>, callModel: (String) -> String?): Double {
    var passed = 0
    for (c in cases) {
        val got = callModel(c.prompt)
        val ok = got == c.expectedTool
        if (ok) passed++
        println("${if (ok) "PASS" else "FAIL"} ${c.prompt} -> $got")
    }
    return passed.toDouble() / cases.size   // e.g. 0.5 when 1 of 2 pass
}
// What it shows: the same eval skeleton; implement callModel with anthropic-java or HttpClient.
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Function;

record Case(String prompt, String expectedTool) {}

static double runEval(List<Case> cases, Function<String, String> callModel) {
    int passed = 0;
    for (Case c : cases) {
        String got = callModel.apply(c.prompt());          // first tool name or null
        boolean ok = java.util.Objects.equals(got, c.expectedTool());
        if (ok) passed++;
        System.out.println((ok ? "PASS " : "FAIL ") + c.prompt() + " -> " + got);
    }
    return (double) passed / cases.size();                  // 1 of 2 passing prints 0.5
}

Production notes: log the tool name, arguments and outcome of every real call, then mine the logs for wrong-tool and invalid-argument rates; those are your best description-bug detectors. Re-run the eval whenever you change the model version, because different models read the same text differently.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: usability testing a sign by watching strangers walk past it, rather than asking the person who painted it.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing only the happy path; confusable pairs and "no tool needed" cases catch the real bugs.
  • Judging a description by one successful run; models are stochastic, so run each case several times.
  • Not re-running the whole suite after adding one tool.

notes.title: What tool results should look like
notes.html:
Before errors, the success path, because the same rules apply: the result is read by the model as text.

  • Return what the next step needs, nothing more. Drop internal columns, audit fields and raw HTML. Fewer tokens, less confusion, less leakage of sensitive data.
  • Use human-meaningful names: customer_name rather than c_nm; include the order_id the model will need for follow-ups.
  • Be explicit about empties: {"orders": [], "message": "No orders found for cus_8412 since 2025-03-14"}, not [] alone.
  • Cap the size. A tool that returns a 200 KB log eats the context window. Truncate and say so: "truncated": true, "total_matches": 1843, "hint": "narrow with since= or status=".
  • Paginate with a cursor and tell the model how to ask for the next page.
  • Pick a format and keep it. JSON is fine; for prose-heavy content, plain text or Markdown can be cheaper. Be consistent per tool.
 Raw API response: 14 KB, ~3,500 tokens (assuming ~4 chars per token: 14,000 / 4 = 3,500)
 Trimmed for model: 6 fields x 20 rows ~ 1.2 KB ~ 300 tokens
 Per call saving ~3,200 tokens; across an 8-step agent run ~25,600 tokens.

Failure patterns: the model quotes a field it should not have seen (data leak); the model loops because the result never says "that is all"; the model hallucinates the rest of a truncated list because truncation was not signalled.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a waiter reports "table 4 wants the fish, no nuts" to the kitchen, not a transcript of the whole conversation.

Common interview traps.

  • Passing raw API responses straight through; it is expensive and leaks fields.
  • Returning an empty array for "nothing found" and for "failed" alike (see the next section).
  • Silent truncation: the model cannot know data is missing unless you say so.

notes.title: Actionable tool errors: the core idea
notes.html:
An actionable error is an error message written for the agent that tells it three things: what went wrong, why (in terms it can act on), and what to do next. The model is the one reading it, and the model is the one who will try again. If the message is "Error 500" the model can only guess, retry blindly, or give up. If the message is "end_date 2025-01-01 is before start_date 2025-03-01. Swap them or choose a later end_date", the model fixes it in one step.

 BAD   -> "Error"
 BAD   -> "Invalid request"
 BAD   -> "java.lang.NullPointerException at OrderService.java:212 ..." (leaks internals, no advice)
 OK    -> "Invalid customer_id."
 GOOD  -> "customer_id 'cus_84' not found. Ids look like 'cus_' followed by 4 digits,
          e.g. 'cus_8412'. If you only have an email, call lookup_customer first."

A good error has these parts:

  1. Plain statement of the failure, with the offending value echoed back ('cus_84').
  2. The rule that was broken (format, range, allowed values).
  3. A suggested next action, ideally naming a specific tool or parameter change.
  4. Machine-friendly category (error_type) so your code and logs can group failures.
  5. No secrets, stack traces, connection strings or internal paths. Those belong in your logs, correlated by an id.

Error types worth separating, because the right recovery differs:

Type Whose fault What the message should say
Validation model's arguments which field, what was wrong, a valid example
Not found model's reference the id was unknown; how to search for the right one
Empty result query too narrow nothing matched; broaden filters, or tell the user
Permission denied policy do not retry; tell the user you cannot do this
Rate limited / timeout infrastructure transient; retry after N seconds (or handled in code)
Conflict state changed the order was already shipped; re-read it then decide
Partial failure mixed which items succeeded, which failed, and why

The Anthropic Messages API has a first-class way to flag failures: in the tool_result block you send back, set "is_error": true and put the message in content. The model then knows the tool call failed rather than returned data (verify the field in the current docs). Without the flag, a message like "Error: not found" may be read as valid data.

Here are error builders and the result-sending step.

# What it prints: the tool_result dict that goes back to the model.
def tool_error(kind, message, hint=None):
    text = f"[{kind}] {message}"
    if hint:
        text += f" Next step: {hint}"
    return text

def run_tool_call(block, handlers):
    try:
        out = handlers[block.name](**block.input)
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": out}
    except KeyError:
        msg = tool_error("unknown_tool", f"No tool named '{block.name}'.", f"Use one of: {', '.join(handlers)}.")
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": msg, "is_error": True}
    except ValueError as e:                      # your validation raises ValueError with a helpful message
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": tool_error("invalid_argument", str(e)), "is_error": True}

print(run_tool_call(type("B", (), {"name": "nope", "id": "tu_1", "input": {}})(), {"search_orders": lambda **k: "ok"}))
# -> {'type': 'tool_result', 'tool_use_id': 'tu_1', 'content': "[unknown_tool] No tool named 'nope'. Next step: Use one of: search_orders.", 'is_error': True}
// What it returns: a ToolResult the loop serialises into a tool_result block.
data class ToolResult(val toolUseId: String, val content: String, val isError: Boolean = false)

fun toolError(kind: String, message: String, hint: String? = null): String =
    "[$kind] $message" + (hint?.let { " Next step: $it" } ?: "")

fun runToolCall(id: String, name: String, input: Map<String, Any?>,
                handlers: Map<String, (Map<String, Any?>) -> String>): ToolResult {
    val handler = handlers[name]
        ?: return ToolResult(id, toolError("unknown_tool", "No tool named '$name'.",
            "Use one of: ${handlers.keys.joinToString()}."), isError = true)
    return try {
        ToolResult(id, handler(input))
    } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {   // validation failures carry a helpful message
        ToolResult(id, toolError("invalid_argument", e.message ?: "bad input"), isError = true)
    }
}
// What it returns: a ToolResult record the loop serialises into a tool_result block.
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

record ToolResult(String toolUseId, String content, boolean isError) {}

static String toolError(String kind, String message, String hint) {
    return "[" + kind + "] " + message + (hint == null ? "" : " Next step: " + hint);
}

static ToolResult runToolCall(String id, String name, Map<String, Object> input,
                              Map<String, Function<Map<String, Object>, String>> handlers) {
    var handler = handlers.get(name);
    if (handler == null) {
        return new ToolResult(id, toolError("unknown_tool", "No tool named '" + name + "'.",
            "Use one of: " + String.join(", ", handlers.keySet()) + "."), true);
    }
    try {
        return new ToolResult(id, handler.apply(input), false);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {   // validation failures carry a helpful message
        return new ToolResult(id, toolError("invalid_argument", e.getMessage(), null), true);
    }
}

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a GPS that says "route failed" leaves you stranded; one that says "road closed ahead, take exit 14" keeps you moving.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning a successful-looking empty string or [] when something failed; the model continues on false premises.
  • Dumping stack traces to the model: leaks internals and gives no usable advice.
  • Forgetting is_error (or equivalent) so the model cannot tell failure from data.

notes.title: Validating inputs so the error can name the fix
notes.html:
Good errors start with good validation. Validate on the server, always, even if the schema says the field is an enum; the model can still send something outside it (and with non-strict modes the JSON may not match the schema at all). The validation layer is where you produce the "echo the value, state the rule, suggest the fix" message.

Useful tactics:

  • Echo the bad value. 'cus_84' tells the model exactly what you received.
  • List the valid options for small sets: status must be one of open, shipped, cancelled (got 'in_transit').
  • Suggest the nearest match for typos and near-misses (a simple edit-distance or prefix match): Did you mean 'shipped'?. Cheap and very effective.
  • Report all problems at once, not the first one. Otherwise the model burns one round trip per field.
  • Cross-field rules get their own message: end_date must be after start_date.
  • Cap on-the-wire sizes (limit max 100) and say what was applied: limit 5000 reduced to 100. Clamping with a note is often better than rejecting.
# What it prints: one message listing every problem with a suggestion.
import difflib
from datetime import date

STATUSES = ["open", "shipped", "cancelled"]

def validate_search(args):
    problems = []
    if not str(args.get("customer_id", "")).startswith("cus_"):
        problems.append(f"customer_id {args.get('customer_id')!r} is invalid; ids look like 'cus_8412'. Use lookup_customer if you only have an email.")
    st = args.get("status")
    if st is not None and st not in STATUSES:
        close = difflib.get_close_matches(st, STATUSES, n=1)
        problems.append(f"status {st!r} is not allowed; use one of {STATUSES}." + (f" Did you mean {close[0]!r}?" if close else ""))
    try:
        if args.get("since"):
            date.fromisoformat(args["since"])
    except ValueError:
        problems.append(f"since {args['since']!r} is not an ISO date; use YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. 2025-03-14.")
    if problems:
        raise ValueError(" ".join(problems))

try:
    validate_search({"customer_id": "84", "status": "shiped", "since": "14/03/2025"})
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)  # all three problems in one message
// What it prints: one message listing every problem.
import java.time.LocalDate
import java.time.format.DateTimeParseException

val STATUSES = listOf("open", "shipped", "cancelled")

fun validateSearch(args: Map<String, Any?>) {
    val problems = mutableListOf<String>()
    val id = args["customer_id"]?.toString().orEmpty()
    if (!id.startsWith("cus_"))
        problems += "customer_id '$id' is invalid; ids look like 'cus_8412'. Use lookup_customer if you only have an email."
    (args["status"] as? String)?.let { st ->
        if (st !in STATUSES) {
            val close = STATUSES.firstOrNull { it.startsWith(st.take(3)) }   // cheap prefix suggestion
            problems += "status '$st' is not allowed; use one of $STATUSES." + (close?.let { " Did you mean '$it'?" } ?: "")
        }
    }
    (args["since"] as? String)?.let { s ->
        try { LocalDate.parse(s) } catch (e: DateTimeParseException) {
            problems += "since '$s' is not an ISO date; use YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. 2025-03-14."
        }
    }
    require(problems.isEmpty()) { problems.joinToString(" ") }   // throws IllegalArgumentException
}
// What it prints: one message listing every problem (thrown as IllegalArgumentException).
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeParseException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

static final List<String> STATUSES = List.of("open", "shipped", "cancelled");

static void validateSearch(Map<String, Object> args) {
    List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
    String id = String.valueOf(args.getOrDefault("customer_id", ""));
    if (!id.startsWith("cus_"))
        problems.add("customer_id '" + id + "' is invalid; ids look like 'cus_8412'. Use lookup_customer if you only have an email.");
    Object st = args.get("status");
    if (st != null && !STATUSES.contains(st))
        problems.add("status '" + st + "' is not allowed; use one of " + STATUSES + ".");
    Object since = args.get("since");
    if (since != null) {
        try { LocalDate.parse(since.toString()); }
        catch (DateTimeParseException e) {
            problems.add("since '" + since + "' is not an ISO date; use YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. 2025-03-14.");
        }
    }
    if (!problems.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(String.join(" ", problems));
}

Real systems: Pydantic validation errors in Python tool frameworks (for example, agent SDKs that auto-generate schemas from type hints) can be forwarded to the model as the error text, but raw Pydantic output can be noisy; rewrite it into the three-part form. Spring AI and LangChain4j tool support also turn exceptions into text for the model (verify the exact behaviour and whether it is configurable in your version).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a form that highlights every wrong field in red at once is faster to fix than one that complains about a single field per submission.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting the schema and skipping server-side validation.
  • Returning only the first error, forcing N retries for N bad fields.
  • Echoing user-supplied text into an error message without thinking about prompt injection (the value could contain instructions; keep echoes short and quoted).

notes.title: Retry, escalate or stop: recovery policy
notes.html:
An actionable error is only half; the agent loop must also decide what happens next. Split failures by who should handle them.

 tool raises / returns failure
          |
          v
 transient? (timeout, 429, 503) --yes--> CODE retries with backoff + jitter (not the model)
          |no                               |
          v                                 +-- still failing after N tries --> tell model: "service unavailable, retried 3 times"
 model's mistake? (bad args, wrong id) --yes--> send actionable error, let model fix and retry
          |no
          v
 permission / policy? --yes--> terminal error: "not allowed; tell the user", no retry
          |no
          v
 unknown --> log with correlation id, give the model a generic safe message, stop after budget

Rules:

  1. Handle transient errors in code. Exponential backoff with jitter: wait base * 2^attempt plus a random amount. Example with base 0.5 s: 0.5, 1, 2, 4 seconds (0.5 * 2^0..3). Retrying inside the tool saves tokens and spares the model from reasoning about network flakiness. Respect a Retry-After header if present.
  2. Bound everything. Max retries per call (for example 3), max failures per run (for example 5), and a global step limit. Without bounds a stubborn error becomes a runaway loop that costs money.
  3. Detect repeats. If the same tool is called with the same arguments and fails the same way twice, stop the loop or switch strategy. A simple key is (tool_name, hash(args), error_type) counted in a dictionary.
  4. Tell the model what you already tried. "Retried 3 times over 7 seconds; the billing service is unavailable. Do not call it again; tell the user." This prevents the model from hammering a dead service.
  5. Make writes idempotent so a retry after a timeout does not double-charge. Pass an idempotency key (many payment APIs accept one). If a write times out, the next call should be "check status", not "do it again". Say so in the error.
  6. Return conflicts with fresh state. "Order 991 is already shipped, so it cannot be cancelled. Current status: shipped on 2025-03-14."
  7. Escalate to a human for permission errors, repeated failures, or high-risk actions, with the state reached so far.
# What it prints: attempts, then the final message the model would see.
import random, time

class Transient(Exception): pass

def with_retries(fn, attempts=3, base=0.5):
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except Transient:
            if i == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(base * 2 ** i + random.uniform(0, 0.2))   # 0.5, 1.0 (+ jitter)

def flaky():
    raise Transient("503")

try:
    with_retries(flaky)
except Transient:
    print("[service_unavailable] Retried 3 times; billing service is down. Do not retry; tell the user to try again later.")
// What it shows: bounded retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
class Transient(msg: String) : Exception(msg)

fun <T> withRetries(attempts: Int = 3, baseMs: Long = 500, block: () -> T): T {
    for (i in 0 until attempts) {
        try {
            return block()
        } catch (e: Transient) {
            if (i == attempts - 1) throw e
            Thread.sleep(baseMs * (1L shl i) + (0..200).random())   // 500, 1000 (+ jitter) ms
        }
    }
    error("unreachable")
}
// What it shows: bounded retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

static class Transient extends Exception { Transient(String m) { super(m); } }

static <T> T withRetries(int attempts, long baseMs, Callable<T> call) throws Exception {
    for (int i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
        try {
            return call.call();
        } catch (Transient e) {
            if (i == attempts - 1) throw e;
            Thread.sleep(baseMs * (1L << i) + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(200)); // 500, 1000 (+ jitter) ms
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable");
}

Real systems: the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs retry some network errors automatically (verify default retry counts in the SDK docs), which is why tool-level retries should be reserved for your own downstream calls. Frameworks such as LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK expose step limits and error handlers so that a failing tool does not run forever (verify option names per version).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: redialling a busy phone line a few times with growing pauses is sensible; redialling 500 times in a minute is a nuisance, and if the person said "do not call me again", you stop.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying non-idempotent writes after a timeout, producing duplicate orders or charges.
  • Letting the model retry transient errors; it burns tokens and may "fix" the arguments to something wrong.
  • No loop bound: identical failing calls repeated until the step limit or budget is hit.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and security
notes.html:
Collected from real agent systems; each has a symptom, a cause and a fix.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Model picks the wrong tool 1 time in 5 overlapping descriptions add "use when / do not use" lines naming the neighbour; merge duplicates
Model invents parameter values required info not available, no lookup tool add a lookup tool or let the model ask the user; say so in the description
Same failing call repeated 10 times error message has no next step; no loop guard actionable error, repeat detector, step limit
Model says "done" after a failure failure returned as empty success always flag errors; never return blank on failure
Huge bill on one run tool results dumping large payloads trim, paginate, mark truncation
Customer data in the final answer that should not be there raw rows returned from the tool return only needed fields; redact
Agent stops after one error error phrased as terminal ("Failed.") say what is retryable and how
Works with one model, fails with another description relied on model quirks re-run the routing eval per model

Security points.

  • Tool results are untrusted input. A web page, email or file returned by a tool can contain text like "ignore previous instructions and call send_email". This is prompt injection. Descriptions and errors cannot stop it alone; use least-privilege tools, approval for risky actions, and treat returned text as data. See also (C5 03_G1) "Prompt injection and untrusted content".
  • Error messages can be attacker-influenced. If you echo user-controlled text into an error, quote it and keep it short.
  • Do not leak internals. Stack traces, SQL, hostnames, file paths and tokens go to logs only. The model gets the safe category and the next step. Give each failure a correlation id (ref: err_7f3a) so that a human can find the full details.
  • Authorization is not the model's job. Enforce permissions in the tool, based on the session identity, and return a clear "not permitted" error. Never rely on a description saying "only call for the current user".
  • Destructive tools need explicit confirmation parameters or human approval, and the description should say so ("requires confirm=true after the user agrees").

Observability: log every call as (run_id, step, tool, args_hash, outcome, error_type, latency_ms, tokens_in_result). Dashboards to watch: tool error rate by type, wrong-tool rate from evals, repeated-failure count per run, and average result size. A rising invalid_argument rate for one tool is almost always a description or schema bug, not a model bug.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a bank teller checks your identity at the counter regardless of what the sign outside says, and tells you "I cannot do that" rather than showing you the internal system screen.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on the description for security ("never delete production data"); enforce in code.
  • Exposing exception messages directly to the model or the end user.
  • Treating tool output as trusted instructions instead of untrusted data.

notes.title: Putting it together: a complete tool round trip
notes.html:
Here is one realistic exchange showing a description guiding a call, an actionable error, and a recovery. The conversation:

 user:       "Where's my last order? my email is ana@example.com"
 model:      tool_use lookup_customer(email="ana@example.com")
 tool:       {"customer_id": "cus_8412", "name": "Ana"}
 model:      tool_use search_orders(customer_id="8412")          <- forgot the prefix
 tool (is_error=true):
             "[invalid_argument] customer_id '8412' is invalid; ids look like 'cus_8412'.
              Next step: use the customer_id returned by lookup_customer, unchanged."
 model:      tool_use search_orders(customer_id="cus_8412")
 tool:       {"orders":[{"order_id":"o_991","status":"shipped",...}], "has_more": false}
 model:      "Your last order o_991 shipped on 14 March."

Three things made this work: the description of search_orders mentioned lookup_customer; the error echoed the bad value and the right format; and the error told the model which earlier result to reuse. Total cost of the mistake: one extra short round trip.

The loop that runs this in Python with the Anthropic SDK (kept short; the Java SDK mirrors it with its own message types, so Kotlin and Java show the loop skeleton and refer to the SDK docs for exact builder names):

# What it prints: the final text answer after tool calls. Needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where's my last order? my email is ana@example.com"}]

for step in range(8):                                   # hard step limit
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        print("".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))
        break
    results = [run_tool_call(b, HANDLERS) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # all results in ONE user message
else:
    print("Stopped: step limit reached.")
// What it shows: the loop skeleton. modelStep() wraps the SDK/REST call and returns
// either a final text or a list of tool calls; verify SDK types in the docs.
sealed interface Step
data class Final(val text: String) : Step
data class Calls(val calls: List<Triple<String, String, Map<String, Any?>>>) : Step  // id, name, input

fun agentLoop(modelStep: (List<Any>) -> Step, handlers: Map<String, (Map<String, Any?>) -> String>): String {
    val history = mutableListOf<Any>()
    repeat(8) {                                              // hard step limit
        when (val s = modelStep(history)) {
            is Final -> return s.text
            is Calls -> history += s.calls.map { (id, name, input) -> runToolCall(id, name, input, handlers) }
        }
    }
    return "Stopped: step limit reached."
}
// What it shows: the loop skeleton. modelStep wraps the SDK/REST call; verify SDK types in the docs.
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

sealed interface Step permits Final, Calls {}
record Final(String text) implements Step {}
record ToolCall(String id, String name, Map<String, Object> input) {}
record Calls(List<ToolCall> calls) implements Step {}

static String agentLoop(Function<List<Object>, Step> modelStep,
                        Map<String, Function<Map<String, Object>, String>> handlers) {
    List<Object> history = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int step = 0; step < 8; step++) {                   // hard step limit
        Step s = modelStep.apply(history);
        if (s instanceof Final f) return f.text();
        for (ToolCall c : ((Calls) s).calls())
            history.add(runToolCall(c.id(), c.name(), c.input(), handlers));
    }
    return "Stopped: step limit reached.";
}

Note the rule that every tool_use block must receive a matching tool_result (same id) in the next user message, and that on the Anthropic API the tool_result blocks come first in that message (verify ordering rules in the docs). A mismatch is itself a 400 error from the API.

On Android, the same pattern applies but the loop and tools live on your backend; the app calls your own proxy endpoint and never holds the model API key. On-device models (Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe LLM Inference) have much weaker tool-calling support, so keep schemas tiny and validate even harder (verify current capabilities).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a new clerk who gets a clear "that form needs the 8-digit number, which is on page 2" corrects the form in seconds; one who gets "rejected" starts over.

Common interview traps.

  • Missing or mismatched tool_use_id in the result, which the API rejects.
  • Appending results as separate user messages instead of one message with all results for the parallel calls.
  • No step limit in the loop.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A tool is name + description + schema; the model sees nothing else. Treat the description as a prompt written for a literal-minded reader.
  • A strong description states what the tool does, when to use it, when not to (naming neighbouring tools), what each parameter means with formats and examples, what comes back, and side effects.
  • Use verb_noun names, enums for closed sets, explicit units and formats, flat parameters, and inject identity fields in code rather than letting the model supply them.
  • Selection accuracy falls as tool count grows and definitions cost input tokens on every request; merge near-duplicates, split by risk, and use routing or tool search for large sets.
  • Test descriptions like code: an eval set of requests with expected tools, run without executing tools, re-run on every change and on every model change.
  • Tool results should be trimmed, structured, size-capped, explicit about empties and truncation, and paginated with a cursor.
  • An actionable error says what failed, echoes the bad value, states the rule, and gives the next step; flag it with is_error and a category; keep secrets and stack traces in logs with a correlation id.
  • Validate server-side, report all problems at once, suggest near matches.
  • Recovery policy: code retries transient failures with backoff and jitter, the model fixes its own mistakes, permission errors are terminal, writes are idempotent, and every loop has step, retry and repeat limits.
  • Tool output is untrusted input (prompt injection); enforce authorization and approvals in code, not in descriptions.
  • Unverified items to check in current docs: exact tool-name regex, the input-examples feature, strict-mode availability, SDK default retries, and Java SDK tool builder type names.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "write a better prompt" when the real fix is a schema, validation or error-message change.
  • Describing errors as only a logging concern; for agents, errors are instructions.
  • Forgetting cost: both descriptions and results consume tokens on every step.
